label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
output:
Here's the reply, as I'd post it:

---

Peter, you've got nine years of payroll behind you and I've read your message twice. I'm not going to stand here and tell you you're wrong — you're right about a good half of it, and one of your points is the reason I run this scheme the way I do now. Where I push back hard is on shutting the window, because we did that in February 2025, with your script almost word for word, and people did not adjust. They adjusted to the loan apps instead. And that cost landed on us in a way that never appeared in a payroll forecast.

**What we did in 2025**

We closed advances in February after Finance pushed. Same three arguments: we're not a bank, the cash flow forecast gets wrecked, some people take one every month. We gave two months' notice, ran one financial literacy session with the SACCO, and shut the window.

I believed the session would carry it. That was the part I got wrong.

**The six months after**

- Debt collector and loan app calls to our office went from a handful to 61 logged by reception.
- Some of those apps were calling our supervisors, who had been listed as "referees" on the loans. So our people were being chased at work, by people quoting names they'd got from our own staff.
- Unplanned absence on the two days after month-end rose. Our fleet manager tied at least three missed runs to drivers who were "sorting out" loans.

That's the thing about closing the window: the cost doesn't go to zero. It moves out of payroll and into operations, reception and the fleet, where nobody is tracking it and nobody can tell the MD where it went.

**Why the apps won**

One financial literacy session doesn't cover a Tuesday afternoon when a child is sent home from school over fees. SACCOs take two to three weeks and need guarantors. A loan app takes ten minutes. So the real choice was never advance or SACCO — it was advance or app, and on speed the app wins every time.

One of our loaders came to me with six apps running at once, borrowing from one to pay the other. It took us four months, working with payroll, to unwind it. And that was the good outcome — he stayed with us.

**What we did instead (September 2025)**

We reopened it as a written policy:

- Maximum 40% of net pay
- Once per pay cycle
- Repaid in full at the next payroll
- No fee
- Requested through the payroll portal, not my office

Before approving anything we check the Employment Act limit on total deductions, which is two-thirds of wages. A 40% ceiling sits well under that, so nobody ends up at month end with nothing and we're never approving a deduction that breaches the Act. On that side of it, we're not a lender — we're a capped, one-cycle, Act-compliant bridge.

**The numbers since we reopened**

- Roughly 55 to 70 requests a month, averaging about KES 9,000.
- 100% recovered, except two leavers. Total written off for the year: about KES 14,000.
- That's the entire cost of the leavers, and I've costed it. What I haven't costed to the penny is the absence and the missed runs, and I won't pretend otherwise — but three missed runs and a visible absence spike is not a rounding error sitting next to KES 14,000.

And here's the part I most want to put in front of Brenda's Finance Manager: our Finance Manager now defends the scheme himself. His objection was never really about advances being wrong in principle, it was about them being a surprise. With a written cap the impact is known in advance. It's a fixed ceiling, not a cliff. At current volumes that's roughly KES 500,000 to KES 630,000 out per cycle — a number he can put in a forecast, phase, or scale down.

**Where I think you're right**

- A salary advance doesn't fix a chronic money shortfall. Anyone who tells you it does is selling something. You're right that some of our people are permanently a month behind, and a policy doesn't change that.
- Recovery when someone leaves is a real problem. It's precisely why we cap at 40% and take it at source in the next cycle. Our actual loss was KES 14,000 for the year.
- The HR hours are real. It's why this runs through the payroll portal and not a conversation in my office. It still needs a monthly reconciliation with payroll; I'm not pretending it's free.
- Financial literacy is worth doing. We kept doing it.
- The people taking an advance every month are still taking one every month. What changed is that it's now inside a rule with a ceiling, and Finance can see by name who's doing it. Under the old informal scheme the same person took one every month and nobody held a record.

**One thing I'd gently push back on**

You said the loan apps are the employee's own decision and their own contract. I understand the principle. But when one of those apps calls our reception, and then calls our supervisor as a referee, the decision has already been made using our premises and our people's names. The loan app alternative is already happening inside the workplace. The difference is that at the moment we don't know the terms, don't know the interest, and don't know who else is being called. A capped advance at least puts a number on it.

**For Brenda, for the 18th**

Brenda, I think your Finance Manager is making two arguments and it's worth separating them, because they need different answers.

If it's a cash flow argument: hand him the ceiling. Offer to start at 25% of net pay for two quarters and review. Give him the cycle number. Give him the recovery record. That objection is answerable on the spot.

If it's a moral argument — "we're not a bank" — then the question to put back to him is: what is the alternative, in numbers? Because the alternative isn't that the need disappears. The alternative is 61 calls in six months, absence after month-end, missed runs, and our supervisors being chased as referees for loans they never took out. That's the version of "not a bank" we ran for six months in 2025.

What I'd propose you put on the table, so he has something concrete to accept or reject:

- **Cap:** 40% of net pay maximum (or 25% for an initial trial period)
- **Frequency:** once per pay cycle
- **Repayment:** in full, deducted at the next payroll, no fee
- **Approval route:** payroll portal, with the Employment Act two-thirds deduction check applied before release
- **Recovery:** single-cycle exposure, so a leaver costs one cycle and nothing more

Peter, if you've seen the reverse work — closing the window and having people genuinely adjust after the session — I'd genuinely like to hear how you handled the calls that came in afterwards, because that was the bit we underestimated. We may have got the policy right and the warning wrong, and I'd rather test that than assume.

Brenda, happy to talk you through the mechanics, and to send the figures in a form you can put in front of the MD on the 18th. It's much easier to argue a number than a feeling.
